claim: Case-management tools and approaches are widely used in programmes seeking to counter radicalisation to violence, but a 2024 Campbell systematic review found no eligible effectiveness evaluations for these interventions, so their effect on violent-radicalisation outcomes cannot currently be established from the reviewed evidence base.

source.title: Case management interventions seeking to counter radicalisation to violence and related forms of violence: A systematic review

study_characteristics.design_note: The review separated effectiveness from implementation. No eligible studies addressed the effectiveness objective for counter-radicalisation case management, while 47 studies examined implementation-related questions.

key_results: No eligible studies were identified that could establish whether case-management tools or approaches reduce radicalisation to violence.

Implementation research identified recurring issues including inconsistent tool use, subjective interpretation of risk, information-sharing and inter-agency coordination challenges, resourcing constraints, and uncertainty about translating assessments into practical action.

Evidence from case management for other forms of violence was also inconclusive overall; reviews of risk-assessment tools and polygraphs reported mixed results, and the review cautions that assessment tools alone would not be expected to directly reduce violence.

Some implementation studies identified skilled practitioners, tailoring support to client needs, trust-building, continuity, and multi-agency working as facilitators, but these implementation observations are not evidence of outcome effectiveness.
why_high_information_value: Counter-radicalisation programmes can be consequential for both violence prevention and civil liberties, so separating widespread use from demonstrated effectiveness is decision-relevant.
The review provides a strong negative-evidence signal: a substantial implementation literature exists without eligible effectiveness evidence for the intervention class.
The record guards against inferring effectiveness from programme logic, practitioner acceptance, risk-assessment infrastructure, or institutional adoption.
limitations: Absence of eligible effectiveness studies is not evidence that case management is ineffective; it means effectiveness could not be determined under the review's inclusion criteria.
The literature search was completed in January 2023, so later evaluations may not be represented.
Case-management programmes vary in target populations, legal settings, voluntariness, assessment tools, practitioner models, service availability, and definitions of radicalisation and violence.
Implementation findings are uneven in quality and should not be promoted into causal claims about violence reduction.

Transferability from case management used for interpersonal or collective violence to counter-radicalisation is conceptually plausible but not equivalent to demonstrated effectiveness in radicalisation contexts.
Counter-radicalisation interventions can create rights, privacy, stigma, discrimination, and trust risks; an effectiveness record alone would not resolve those normative or distributional questions.
This candidate does not establish cost-effectiveness or HumanityAI's comparative advantage in supporting, opposing, or designing such programmes.
counterevidence_and_uncertainty: Forty-seven implementation studies indicate that case-management practice is not an evidence-free field; useful implementation knowledge exists even though outcome-effectiveness evidence is absent under the review criteria.
Some studies judged intervention assumptions to align with academic research, but plausible programme logic is not a substitute for outcome evaluation.
The review found mixed and inconclusive evidence for related case-management tools in other violence domains, so neither a broad positive nor broad null effectiveness conclusion is warranted.
recommended_integration: After independent source verification and a check for post-January-2023 effectiveness evaluations, consider an insufficient-evidence P01/P08/P10 record emphasizing that widespread implementation and programme logic must not be treated as proof of violence-prevention effectiveness.
